## Week 4: optimization and model fitting

How a model actually gets fitted. Logistic regression first: maximum likelihood, the score equations read as week 2's orthogonality, and why there is no closed form. Then the method that fits almost everything else: gradient descent, step sizes and the descent lemma, and its stochastic version, whose random steps are unbiased for the full gradient. Empirical risk minimization as the common form of every method so far, the bias--variance decomposition in that form, why no method is best on every problem, and early stopping as a first kind of regularization.

**Reading**

- PPA Chapter 5 (Optimization), from "Optimization basics" through "The SGD quick start guide", pp. 70–86, stopping at "Analysis of the stochastic gradient method": gradient descent, the quadratic case, and stochastic gradient descent in practice.

Optional: PPA "Analysis of the stochastic gradient method", pp. 86–88 (a convergence bound), and "Regularization" with "Implicit regularization by optimization", pp. 92–94 (why gradient descent from zero lands on the minimum-norm solution, which the seminar meets); ESL section 4.4.1 for Newton-IRLS in full; the Wikipedia pages on [Newton's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_method_in_optimization) and [gradient descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent) for pictures and animations.

**Lecture:** [slides](weeks/04-optimization/slides/04-1-optimization.html)

**Seminar:** [notebook](weeks/04-optimization/notebooks/notebook4.html) ([.qmd](https://ml4ds.com/weeks/04-optimization/notebooks/notebook4.qmd){download="notebook4.qmd"}) · [notebook with solutions](https://ml4ds.com/solutions/notebook4_solutions.html). Before the seminar, do exercises 1 to 4 at the top of the notebook (the lecture's descent lemma again with the slides closed, the ERM form of the bias--variance decomposition, the logistic Hessian and the Newton-Raphson update, and no free lunch on a finite domain); the seminar's problems start from them. You write gradient descent once, as a function, and use it for least squares, logistic regression and random batches. Data: gapminder and the Palmer penguins ([data note](data/penguins.html)), then simulated data.
